text:
Abraham is commanded to take his son, his only son, whom he loves; and of what Abraham felt upon hearing the command we are told nothing whatever. The narrator never looks into his mind. He does not protest; he does not bargain; there is no trace in him of the man who pleaded with God for Sodom, and who would have spared the city for the sake of ten righteous. In this chapter Abraham is less a character, in the sense in which we speak of characters in a play, than a silence, and I take that silence to be the very meaning of the episode. The reader is left with a question which the narrator raises and does not answer.

The three days of travel may be read as a kind of suspended sentence. Outwardly nothing happens in them; inwardly everything happens. The narrator dwells upon the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire, and so names the instruments of the act before the act itself is come to. Obedience and horror are kept side by side through the whole story, and neither is ever suffered to prevail over the other. Faith, as it appears here, has nothing of feeling in it; it is rather a geometry, a matter of lines drawn and distances kept.

We must remember that Isaac is the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; and it is this very promise that is turned into a test. When we recall the earlier promise, the distance between promise and test grows less, until the two can scarcely be told apart. The scene turns upon a single word, hineni, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: to God, to Isaac, and to the angel. Each time the word means something different, and each time it costs him more than before. To declare himself present is, for Abraham, to be bound up with loss.

What does Isaac know? We are not told. He carries the wood; he asks about the lamb; he receives an answer which is no answer at all. Of his thoughts the narrator gives no account. The question of his consent is raised and then quietly laid aside, unresolved; and obedience, reckoned strictly, leaves nothing over. There is only a verb, and a phrase that recurs, as if repetition could stand in the place of explanation: they went, both of them, together.

A reader who attends to what is missing will be rewarded. Sarah is absent from the chapter entirely, and her death is announced in the verse which immediately follows it. We are led to suspect, though nowhere told, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants; of Isaac there is no mention. The narrator turns away at precisely the moment when a lesser story would linger, and a good part of the meaning lies in what he omits. Such silence is itself a kind of testimony; we hear it in the empty place where Isaac's name should stand.

It may be objected that this reticence belongs merely to the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains. In some sense this may be true. Yet the same narrator, elsewhere, tells us plainly what his people feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence in this place is therefore deliberate, and not the accident of a manner. Restraint, in such a writer, becomes a kind of accusation; and it is the more severe because Esau's cry and Joseph's tears are left on record.

The narrator does not reconcile the God who promises with the God who demands; he sets them down together and does not choose between them. Abraham stands on the mountain with the knife raised, and the ram not yet seen; and the reader is left in the same place. The question admits of no answer, and I am persuaded that its want of an answer is the only answer we shall have. To read the chapter is to be tested by it, as Abraham was tested.

Genesis 22, then, is less a story about sacrifice than a story about reading; and what it teaches is that the most important things are those which a writer declines to say. Abraham is silent; Isaac asks his question; Sarah is absent; the narrator will not explain. Each of these is a gap in the account, and each gap makes its demand upon us. The brevity of the chapter lays its burden upon the reader, so that what is withheld is precisely what is given; and the heaviest part of that burden is the single verse, set just beyond the mountain, in which Sarah dies.
